source.facts: Confirmed by Winston (Nov 2026): only designer; worked with founders, engineers and ops/marketing; Jan–Apr 2026; Yelo's earlier app (Old page) was live; its home was too crowded, social felt bolted on, dated look; the founders picked among directions A–D; B's layout went forward because booking stays first, combined with A; reaction counts were dropped because they felt tacky and few people would tap them (they came from an earlier iMessage-based version where people reacted to ride requests); feed-card changes were his own judgment; home + feed, search + map, ride options and onboarding are live; vehicles sketched first, then modelled and iterated with Gemini, generated together for consistency; no usage numbers. Takeaways he chose: old habits inform design; booking first, social second; simplifying a crowded home. Follow-up: worked with a PM and ops (not marketing); iOS only. Depth round: sky gradient = neutral, calm, people heading out; sky tinted by service status was dropped so home wouldn't scream the app isn't working, status moved to the LIVE pill; yellow limited to point to the main action, let event art stand out, because the brand colour is loud, and cleaner than the old app; initials for privacy, calmer feed, consistent look; card wording heavily debated, labels for scanning mixed card types, MUTUAL builds trust, bubbly gradient cards nod to text messages; named classes match the real fleet and Exclusive/Shared was confusing; 3D vehicles are abstract because drivers' personal cars all differ. Final designs: section V1.2 (1:5727). Onboarding round: phone first because it's the login, drivers need to reach you, it's a quick start, and the founders required it; school Google/Microsoft sign-in replaced the school picker + emailed code for fewer steps, because schools use them, to pre-fill the profile and keep it students-only; profile pre-filled (less typing); photo optional for riders, required for drivers (photo only where it matters, lower drop-off); welcome shows the app to show the social side early and set Yelo apart; permission reasons build trust, especially contacts. Final designs are section V1.2 (1:5727). Copy round (Nov 2026): don't mention usage numbers; each case ends with a short Summary. Sign-up (Nov 2026): school Google/Microsoft sign-in, with the emailed code as a fallback. Iterations (Nov 2026): Winston asked to bring back the 30+ home screen iterations image as wireframe frames on a dot grid.

fields.description: Redesigning a live campus ride-share app: booking first, social second.
fields.intro: Yelo is a student-only campus ride-share. As the only designer at the time, I redesigned its live rider app, from the home screen to ride options and onboarding.
fields.summary: How might we make Yelo’s social side part of getting a ride, without slowing booking down?
fields.overview: I was the only designer at the time, working with the founders, engineers and the wider team. The founders picked the home direction; the feed card changes were my own calls.
fields.impact: The redesign is live: home and feed, search and map, ride options and onboarding.

sections.title: Problem
sections.heading: A crowded home on a live app
content: Yelo’s earlier app was already live. Three things weren’t working on its home:

bullets: The home was too crowded.
Social features felt bolted on.
The look felt dated.

content.alt: Two iPhones: Yelo’s earlier home with a dark photo header, ticker and hotness scores, and the redesigned home with search first and feed cards for where people are headed, tickets and trending searches
content.caption: Before: the earlier home. After: the redesign.

sections.title: Four directions
sections.heading: Four ways to lay out the home screen
content: My early sketches asked one question: what’s the best way to show that a place is popular?

notes.text: A location colour or icon circle

content.alt: Hand-drawn wireframes of two Yelo home screens and three ways to mark a popular location
content.caption: Early sketches: three ways to mark a popular place.

content: Then I went through more than 30 versions of the home screen.

content.alt: Eight Yelo home screen iterations as outlined frames on a dot grid, from a plain search box to the final home with a live social feed
content.caption: Eight of the 30+ home screen iterations, from a plain search box to the final home.

content: Four of the home layouts I explored became directions A to D:

bullets: **A:** feed first, with search in a bottom sheet.
**B:** search first, with cards below.
**C:** the feed as chat bubbles with reactions.
**D:** a ranked list of popular places.

content.alt: Four iPhones showing Yelo home directions: feed first, search first, chat bubbles, ranked list
content.caption: A, B, C and D.

content: The founders picked the direction. V1 mixed B and A:

bullets: **B’s layout:** booking stays first, so search sits at the top.
**A’s live row:** “Someone is searching for a ride…”

**No reaction counts:** they came from an earlier version that ran through iMessage, where we noticed people reacting to each other’s ride requests. But they felt a bit tacky, and we didn’t think many people would tap them.

content.alt: An iPhone showing the Yelo V1 home: search first, a Someone is searching for a ride row, and feed cards without reaction counts
content.caption: V1 home.

sections.title: Feed card
sections.heading: A card that says who and where
content: After V1, I kept changing the feed card. These were my own calls:

bullets: “Ride to” became “Headed to”.
“Someone you may know” became a MUTUAL tag.
Labels for each kind of signal came in one at a time: HEADED TO, then TRENDING SEARCH, then GOT TICKETS.

content.alt: Four iPhones showing the Yelo feed card change: Ride to cards, Headed to cards with initials, a MUTUAL tag, and labelled cards
content.caption: Left to right: V1 to the latest card.

content: The wording was heavily debated. Each card had to catch just the right amount of attention. Showing searches, where people are going and events gives people a reason to care about the social side, which is the point of a social ride-share.

bullets: **Labels** let you scan a feed that now mixes rides, tickets and searches.
**MUTUAL** shows someone in common, which builds trust.
**Initials instead of photos** for privacy, a calmer feed and a consistent look.
**Soft, slightly bubbly cards** with a light gradient nod to text messages, while staying clean and not overpowering.

content.alt: A close-up of four Yelo feed cards: HEADED TO, GOT TICKETS, TRENDING SEARCH and a HEADED TO card with a MUTUAL tag, each with a coloured initials avatar
content.caption: Labels, MUTUAL and initials in the latest cards.

sections.title: Ride options
sections.heading: Three versions of the ride sheet
content: The ride sheet went from Exclusive vs. Shared with a seat stepper, to ETA first, to four named vehicle classes with one tag each.

content.alt: Three iPhones showing Yelo ride sheet versions: Exclusive or Shared with a seat stepper, ETA first, and named vehicle classes with 3D cars
content.caption: Ride sheet versions, left to right.

bullets: **Named classes match Yelo’s real fleet,** which includes carts and mini buses, not just cars.
**Exclusive vs. Shared wasn’t clear.**

content.alt: A close-up of the Yelo ride options: Car, Big Car, Cart and Mini Bus, each with a 3D vehicle, price and one tag
content.caption: Four classes, one tag each.

content: Drivers use their own cars, and they’re all different, so a photo of “the car” would be wrong. The 3D vehicles are an abstract, fun stand-in.

I sketched the vehicles first, then used Gemini to model and iterate on them. I started with one vehicle at a time, then switched to generating them all in one image because it gave more consistent results.

content.alt: Five yellow 3D vehicles in a row: sedan, SUV, golf cart with a flag, van and bus
content.caption: The Yelo fleet.

sections.title: Look and feel
sections.heading: A calm sky, yellow for action

bullets: **A light sky gradient** keeps the app neutral and calm, and hints at people heading out.
**Yellow only marks the main action and LIVE.** Event posters are already colourful, a lot of yellow is hard to read, and the old app used a lot of colour at once.

content: We tried tinting the sky with service status: green on a busy night, orange or red when there weren’t enough drivers or Yelo wasn’t running. We dropped it because we didn’t want the home screen to scream “the app isn’t working right now”. Service status lives in the small pill that usually says LIVE.

content.alt: Three iPhones: Yelo home with a green Busy night for drivers sky, a red Currently not available sky, and the final home with a LIVE pill
content.caption: Tried: tinting the sky by service status. Kept: the LIVE pill.

content.alt: A close-up of the Yelo search bar: Where to? with a yellow LIVE pill
content.caption: The LIVE pill carries service status.

sections.title: Onboarding
sections.heading: Sign-up that gets you riding
content: The final sign-up has seven short steps: welcome, phone number, a text code, student status, a pre-filled profile, an optional photo and permissions.

content.alt: Three iPhones: the Yelo welcome screen, the phone number step and Claim your student status with Google or Microsoft
content.caption: Welcome, phone number, student status.

bullets: **Phone first.** Your phone number is your login, drivers need to reach you, and it’s the quickest way to start. It was also a requirement from the founders.

**School Google or Microsoft sign-in** replaced the old school picker. It’s fewer steps, most students already have one of those accounts, it keeps Yelo students-only, and it fills in the profile. An emailed code is still there as a fallback.
**The welcome screen shows the app,** with the feed, events and deals, so the social side is clear before you sign up and Yelo doesn’t read as just another ride-share.

content.alt: Three iPhones: the pre-filled Yelo profile, the optional profile picture step, and permissions with a reason for each
content.caption: Pre-filled profile, optional photo, permissions.

bullets: **Confirm, don’t type.** The profile comes pre-filled from the school account.
**The photo is optional for riders** and only used in social features. Drivers have to add one. Fewer required steps means fewer people drop off.
**Every permission says why.** Reasons build trust, especially for contacts.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.heading: What shipped
content: Home and feed, search and map, ride options and onboarding are live.

bullets: **Old habits inform design.** People already reacted to each other’s ride requests in the iMessage version, and that’s where reactions came from.
**Booking first, social second.** Social signals only help if they don’t slow down getting a ride.
**Simplify a crowded home.** A lot of the work was deciding what to leave out, like reaction counts and the status-tinted sky.

content: Yelo’s earlier app was live, but its home was crowded, social features felt bolted on, and the look was dated. I explored four home directions, and the founders went with B’s layout, combined with parts of A, so booking stays first.

I reworked the feed cards so mixed card types are easy to scan. I swapped Exclusive and Shared for named vehicle classes that match the real fleet. And sign-up got shorter, with a profile that fills itself in from your school account. Search now sits at the top of home, and the feed underneath shows where people are headed, who got tickets and what’s trending.
